title: Twice as Often
concept: Four typographic beats set the Voynich manuscript's counted statistics, from its word total to Zipf's one-over-rank sizes, its predictable glyphs and its parchment date.

mechanism_embodied.how_visualised: In the second beat the words first, second and third are set at type sizes in the ratio 1 : 1/2 : 1/3 beneath the heading 1 / rank, so the size falloff is the frequency falloff. The other beats carry the word count, the entropy finding and the radiocarbon date as headline and subline pairs.

discarded_obvious_idea: Setting fake Voynich-like glyphs in a manuscript pastiche was discarded: it decorates the mystery but shows none of the statistics, and invented glyphs would misrepresent the script.
motion_sound_plan: No sound. Two background bands of monospaced labels scroll in opposite directions. Each beat's headline slides in, fades up over one second, drifts left and fades out before the next. The Zipf words rise into place one after another. Under prefers-reduced-motion the clock runs at one fifth speed.

storyboard.description: 38,000 words, about 9,000 different, on some 240 pages; the band reads BEINECKE MS 408.
first, second, third rise at sizes 1, 1/2, 1/3 above the heading 1 / rank.
easy to guess: the next glyph is unusually predictable, unlike every comparison text.
1404 to 1438, the parchment's radiocarbon date, held with the bands still scrolling.

memorable_moment: The word first set in rust at full size with second and third shrinking beside it.
self_declared_risk: A wider fallback serif could push the long sublines toward the right edge on narrow or unusual viewports.
liner_note: The Voynich manuscript, Beinecke MS 408, holds roughly 38,000 words, about 9,000 of them different, and nobody can read them. Counting still works. The most common word appears about twice as often as the second and three times as often as the third, the falloff Zipf's law predicts for real languages, so the second beat sets first, second and third at those relative sizes. Lindemann and Bowern found the opposite at the letter level: glyph sequences are unusually predictable, and in their study Voynichese differed from every comparison text. Radiocarbon dating puts the parchment between 1404 and 1438.
